OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Is there an infinite Lucas sequence $a_0,a_1,\ldots$ where $a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n$ for $n\geq 0$ such that all $a_k$ are composite, and yet no integer has a common factor with every term of the sequence?
#276: [ErGr80,p.27]
number theory | 
covering systems
Whether such a composite Lucas sequence even exists was open for a while, but using covering systems Graham [Gr64] showed that\[a_0 = 1786772701928802632268715130455793\]and\[a_1 = 1059683225053915111058165141686995\]generate such a sequence. This problem asks whether one can have a composite Lucas sequence without 'an underlying system of covering congruences responsible'. 
This problem has been 'conjecturally solved' by Ismailescu and Son [IsSo14], in that they provide an explicit infinite Lucas sequence in which all the terms are composite, and believe that no covering system is responsible for this. See the comment by van Doorn below for more details.
See also [1113] for another problem in which the question is whether covering systems are always responsible.
Additional thanks to: Dogmachine and Wouter van Doorn

 The smallest known pair of starting values for which a Graham-type Lucas sequence exists, was gradually brought down by Knuth, Wilf, Nicol and Vsemirnov, with the latter holding the current record with $a_0 = 106276436867$ and $a_1 = 35256392432$ (despite Erdős and Graham writing 'it would be very surprising if a pair existed with both components less than $10^{20}$' in [ErGr80]!). So these starting values lead to a Lucas sequence which, thanks to a covering system, only contains composite values. Fun fact: in what feels like an hommage to Graham, the papers by Knuth, Nicol and Vsemirnov all have almost the same title A (new) Fibonacci-like sequence of composite numbers, which was also the title of Graham's original paper. Wilf's example can be found on the OEIS as A083216.
As for a Lucas sequence of composite integers without an underlying covering system (i.e. the question at hand), this was conjecturally solved by Ismailescu and Son in this paper (appropriately titled A new kind of Fibonacci-like sequence of composite numbers), where you can find references to the aforementioned papers as well. 
With $p = 1$, $q$ a $129$-digit monstrosity (see Theorem 3 on page 6 of their paper), $a_0 = p^2 + q^2$, $a_1 = 2pq + q^2$ and $a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} + a_n$ for all $n \ge 0$, Ismailescu and Son prove the following:
1) There exists a positive integer $m$ (for which all its prime factors are smaller than $a_0$) such that $\gcd(m, a_{2n}) > 1$ for all $n \ge 0$. That is, all even-indexed terms are composite thanks to a covering system.
2) For all $n \ge 0$ we have $a_{2n+1} = (pF_n + qF_{n+1})(pL_n + qL_{n+1})$ with $F_n$ and $L_n$ the Fibonacci and Lucas numbers respectively. In particular, all odd-indexed terms are composite too.
Now, as for these odd-indexed terms, there seems to be no reason to believe that a covering system is responsible here as well. However, they are not actually able to prove the non-existence of an $m$ such that $\gcd(m, a_{2n+1}) > 1$ holds for all $n \ge 0$. So that is why one could say that this problem is conjecturally solved.
I do wonder if it's possible to use the ideas in Hough's theorem and follow-up work, to reduce deciding whether a covering system is responsible for the odd-indexed terms in the above example, to a finite computation.
PS. Due to Dogmachine's comment the assumption on the coprimality of $a_0$ and $a_1$ was removed. However, this assumption is of course important for Graham's example.
